audience: Engineers who know autoregressive generation and need a concrete latency model.
prerequisites: One target pass produces a next-token distribution.
A speculative proposal is not committed output.
objective: Explain why the same three-token accepted prefix can arrive earlier on a shared clock even when sequential drafting overhead is included.
scope: All-accepted sequential drafting, one shared illustrative clock; rejection and any additional target token are deliberately outside this prefix-availability comparison.
assumptions: Three target passes cost one toy time unit each.
Three sequential draft steps cost 0.2 units each; one batched verification costs one.
Both lanes use the same horizontal scale; opening camera zoom is not latency.
All three proposed tokens can, reason, fast are accepted. No measured speedup is claimed.
Presentation seconds and algorithm time units are distinct. Narration may exceed a storyboard target without changing algorithm costs.
Duration ranges are authored review bands around the README's approximate presentation spans, not measured speech durations or hard cuts.
unknowns: No learner responses or audiovisual inspection are bundled. Recorded completion events locate key transitions for review; their presence is not a certificate of rendered fidelity or comprehension.

claims.statement: Autoregressive target decoding of three tokens requires three serial target steps; speculative execution permits concurrency when guesses can be reused.

evidence.locator: Section 1, opening paragraphs and speculative execution discussion
evidence.support: The introduction explicitly distinguishes K serial target runs from speculative concurrency; it does not supply this scene's toy durations.

claims.statement: The displayed three-token prefix completes at 3 baseline units versus 1.6 speculative units, including 0.6 drafting units.

evidence.support: ToyTiming defines 1.0 target, 0.2 draft and 1.0 verification costs. One EventTimeline supplies both lanes; independent arithmetic below checks totals.

claims.statement: The comparison illustrates the all-accepted case rather than universal acceleration or a complete rejection-sampling algorithm.

evidence.support: Narration says all three are accepted; the picture labels time illustrative and costs are documented as not measured.

worked_examples.description: Compute baseline and speculative completion from input costs, without importing ToyTiming or graphical coordinates.

beats.purpose: A target work boundary finishes before the first token appears.

narration.text: Watch the waiting. The next token cannot start until this target pass finishes.

beats.purpose: Two further dependent target passes release the rest of the prefix.

narration.text: Then another pass. And another. Three tokens, three expensive waits.

beats.purpose: Include three sequential cheap steps on the same clock.

narration.text: Now keep the same clock. A small draft model proposes three tokens, one after another.

beats.purpose: Outlined markers remain guesses until verification.
One verification boundary spans all proposed positions.

narration.text: One target pass checks the proposed positions together.

beats.purpose: The same markers become accepted at 1.6; the shared scale reveals saved waiting.

narration.text: Here, all three are accepted. The same prefix is ready sooner, even including drafting.

transfer_questions.question: Keeping three accepted tokens and verification cost one, what if each draft step costs 0.8 units?
transfer_questions.expected_answer: Speculation completes at 3.4 units, slower than the baseline's 3; acceptance alone does not guarantee a speedup.
transfer_questions.justification: Three sequential draft steps cost 3 times 0.8 = 2.4, followed by one verification unit. The baseline still costs three units. These are input-cost arithmetic, not measured latencies.

transfer_questions.question: If the last narration block takes twelve seconds, does the algorithm now cost twelve time units?
transfer_questions.expected_answer: No. Narration seconds are presentation timing; the toy speculative completion remains 1.6 units. Review and explain the pacing rather than cutting speech or relabeling cost.
transfer_questions.justification: ToyTiming computes algorithm coordinates from work costs. The narrate tracker separately budgets presentation time; neither changes the other's unit system.
